title: Flash sale inventory
like: a limited-stock sale like a sneaker drop
brief: At noon a hot item goes on sale with only a few thousand units. A huge crowd arrives in the same minute and everyone taps Buy. Stock must never go below zero, nobody should be charged for an item that is gone, and the site must not fall over.

clarify.q: Can we sell more than we have?
clarify.a: Never. Overselling means cancelled orders and angry buyers.

clarify.q: Must buyers get an instant answer?
clarify.a: They need to know their order was received within a second. Confirmation can follow shortly after.

clarify.q: Can some buyers be turned away?
clarify.a: Yes. Stock is tiny compared with the crowd, so most people will see "sold out". That is fine if it is fast and honest.

notes: Only about 5,000 units are for sale, but about 7,500 buy attempts a second arrive at the first minute (approx.).
One item row is the hot key everyone fights over.

hints: Millions fight over one number: the units left. What makes the count safe, and what keeps the crowd away from it?
Rate limit the crowd at the edge, then put buy attempts in a queue so one worker at a time touches the stock. Browsing can come from a cache.
CDN and cache for the page, a rate limiter, servers, a queue, workers with an idempotency store, a SQL database that takes stock in one step.

editorial.summary: Keep the crowd and the stock apart. A cache and CDN absorb browsing, a rate limiter trims the bots, and buy attempts wait in a queue. A few workers take stock one transaction at a time, so the count never goes wrong and the database is never swarmed.

designs.name: Queue in front of one safe stock counter
designs.why: The queue turns a crowd into an orderly line. Workers check the idempotency store, then take stock in one SQL transaction. Everyone past the stock gets a quick sold-out answer.

tradeoffs: A queue gives a "received" answer fast and protects the stock, but the final yes or no arrives a moment later.
Rate limiting at the edge keeps bots out, but a strict limit can also turn away real buyers on a shared network.
One database row for stock is simple and correct. Splitting the stock over many rows is faster but adds care when it runs low.
Holding an item in the cart for a few minutes is kind to buyers but locks stock that may never be paid for.
editorial.realWorld: Limited drops can bring hundreds of thousands of shoppers in one minute for a few thousand units. Big retailers put waiting rooms and queues in front of the stock for this reason (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Two orders claim the last unit and one payment times out. What inventory transaction and payment states prevent overselling or charging twice?
correctness.discussion: Reserve stock with an atomic conditional decrement only when enough remains, and bind the reservation to a unique order id. Retries return the existing order. Track reserved, paid and released states; release only the reservation still owned by that order. Use a stable provider idempotency key for payment. A timeout is an unknown outcome, so reconcile before retrying or releasing. Refund a late success if the reservation was already released.
